newsitem.title: USA: US lawmakers offer bill to halt new Internet taxes.
newsitem.headline: US lawmakers offer bill to halt new Internet taxes.

text.p: Two lawmakers on Thursday offered a bill aimed at preventing state and local governments from imposing a torrent of new taxes that target the Internet and the business conducted over the global computer network.

The bill, offered by Sen. Ron Wyden, an Oregon Democrat, and Rep. Chris Cox, a California Republican, also calls on the Clinton administration to develop a broad plan to address the issue of electronic commerce taxes.
The bill would impose an indefinite moratorium on state and local taxes on electronic commerce.
But the ban would not apply to normal business income taxes, "fairly apportioned" business license taxes and sales taxes that also apply to interstate mail order and telephone orders.

Businesses, particularly entrepreneurial ones, have been struggling with a variety of tax proposals from state and local governments, which increasingly view the Internet as a potential "cash cow" for tax revenues, Wyden said at a news conference.
By the year 2000, commerce on the Internet is expected to reach $600 billion a year, according to some estimates.
"Many people are looking at the World Wide Web as a 'world wide wallet,'" Cox said of state, county and municipal governments.

In addition to state and local sales taxes, some states are imposing taxes for hooking up to the Internet. And nearly every state's approach to electronic commerce taxes varies, causing problems for companies doing business over a global network.
The Clinton administration last November said that no special taxes should be imposed in cyberspace.
It also said in a report that the Treasury Department is not considering any new type of value added tax, "bit" tax, or other new excise tax on electronic commerce.
The new legislation has the backing of various business groups, including the American Electronics Association.

"The current confusion and lack of certainty over potential tax liabilities is a great inhibitor to the growth of the electronic marketplace," said William Archey, president of the high-tech industry trade group.
